Five Nights at Freddy's is an awesome little indie game that's become very popular in a short span of time. The gameplay is simple - you're in a room and have the ability to control the lights and doors of your office as well as the ability to monitor the cameras dotted around the building. You need to keep an eye on the four animatronics that will move around and kill you if they manage to enter your office. To make things more difficult, you have a very limited amount of power which is drained more quickly if you keep lights turned on and doors closed, effectively meaning you need to leave yourself exposed if you want to survive. 

As a horror game, it works very well. The robots are suitably unnerving and the game makes you extremely paranoid thanks to the lighting and sound effecs. There's nothing unfair about the game - if you can keep your cool and use your resources effectively, you'll be fine, but more often than not the player will end up panicking and being punished for it. The atmosphere and story are fantastic as well - the messages and notes left behind for the player all add up to create a very enigmatic yet creepy story that people are still speculating on, combined with numerous other easter eggs.

The developer seems down to earth and willing to listen to his fans, and has already promised a sequel. I would recommend buying the game to support him for this reason and so that we can hopefully see more games like this. The game is not huge, but it's a great addition to the horror genre and is definitely something all horror fans should want to see more of in a sea of action games and zombies.

Iconic game. Big part of my childhood. I miss the times when everyone was watching their favourite youtubers playing it, making theories, SFM's and AMV's. Incredible era. I'm thankful to grow up in it.

Five Nights at Freddy's is an Indie point-and-click horror game that literally bombed the Steam Store on its very first month of purchase and is infamously known as a breath of fresh air for games that plays along the themes of tension and paranoia. It is also most known amongst fans that famous Youtube personalities such as Markiplier and PewDiePie have made the sales of this game boost even higher than usual indie game sales. As a small synopsis related to this game, you'll be waddling through Freddy's game of don't-hide-but-seek, right to the very perilous end.

With only little power reserved for poor old Mike Schmidt in the Security Guard's Office of Freddy Fazbear's Pizza; a family restaurant complex, you'll be struggling to stay alive and out of danger on your six hour night shift of work, starting from 12 AM to 6 AM for five days straight, hence the title of the game. With every night progressively getting worse in both sudden fear and paranoia. The repulsive animatronics that run alive during the night become much more unpredictable, with unexpected jump scares that will leave your heart to skip a beat and without a doubt, make you want to rage quit the game as quickly as possible. You will be having to deal with Freddy and his fearsome buddies, Bonnie the Bunny, Chica the Chicken and Foxy the Pirate Fox. Cute names with horrific intentions.

Inspired by the beloved restaurant, Chuck E. Cheese, now, the deepest nightmares of those kids have come to life as these animatronics in game don't want to sing you no birthday song or throw you a party; they simply plan to crush your body into a mascot costume, completely mashing, fracturing and probably suffocating you in the process. Pretty gruesome way to go.

What makes this game very intriguing is the community's efforts on theorising the deeper meanings of the game's overall plot in context. Ranging from how the phone guy is the actual killer, to Foxy being a good animatronic rather than a bad one. This is all deeming down and shredding away the shady structure of the story that makes us think in our own individual experience. I love the community's reasons for that as it takes devotion and well-thought ingenuity to piece together the mysteries that still lingers on, even to this day.

The game honestly doesn't become as scary as you may think. If you have been playing for hours upon end, it becomes somewhat highly addictive in a sense. Not about to drop any spoilers as such, but after the main five nights, you have an optional 6th night and even after that, you can proceed to the insane 20/20/20/20 difficulty mode, where you're doomed from the very start, unless you can manage to live through it that is.

This game actively toys around with your delusions, as you will franctically switch the lights on and shut the doors in the much more frightening and dangerous nights ahead. Things begin to get real hectic as odd noises protrude from various locations in the restaurant, from the animatronics humming, to random musical tunes seemingly played out of nowhere, to loud footsteps and of course, the demonic laughter. You never know if Bonnie and Chica are ganging up on you or even worse, if you can't turn the lights on or shut the doors, knowing you're doomed with an eventual jumpscare at the end. Even Foxy begins to act creepy, since he's the biggest reserved essence of paranoia for me; you never know his patterns directly and you're left shook up if or when you witness his hasteful run down the hall, leaving you only precious seconds to slam the emergency door down, or else you'll be greeted with an expected jumpscare and a game over.

Definitely recommend this game, and the time I recommend to play this game perfectly fits at midnight, all alone in the dark. I bloody dare you and if you have completed this game, congratulations! Move onto the even more scarier sequels that wait up ahead, brave soul. It's about to get a whole lot more nightmarish.

After 10 years, I finally made it through the five nights and got my $120.

I played this game years ago but could never get past night four.

I've never really been a big fan of the gameplay, and have always found it more fun to watch others play it.

but today I decided to give it another try and I managed to complete the five nights

Little help for completing the game
Small Guide:

Main Objective:
in the beginning itll be a lot more friendly with the animatronics and them attacking but your main objective is left light right light then cam 4b (always stay on 4b unless your trying to stop freddy sooner) 4b is the last location freddy will show before being able to make it into your office. Foxy will be stalled only by checking the cameras very important to remember FOXY DOES NOT REQUIRE YOU TO LOOK AT HIM. Bonnie and Chica are both one and the same thats why you have to check both left then right before camming back to 4b. Every animatronic runs on 5s intervals based on my knowledge so just make sure your doing this method quick and precise. FNAF 1 has the longest nights so its going to be the most difficult to stay locked in. As long as your doing 

left light->right light-> Cam 4b-> repeat 

in under 5s intervals you should be able to beat the game all 3 stars 

Things to remember:

FOXY DOES NOT REQUIRE YOU TO LOOK AT HIM IN CAMS TO STALL

FREDDY APPEARS LAST AT 4B SO MAKE SURE CAMS STAY THERE

ALWAYS CHECK LEFT AND RIGHT BEFORE CAMMING DUE TO BONNIE AND CHICA 

IN ORDER TO CHECK FOXY WHILE FREDDY IS AT 4B CLOSE RIGHT DOOR BEFORE CHECKING FOXING HEARING FREDDYS LAUGH THEN OPENING THE DOOR AGAIN TO REPEAT CYCLE
Honestly, this could all end in under a minute if they would let me just chain them to the stage.

This game will always hold a special place in my heart until the day I die. It was one of my first biggest obsessions as a child, and even now it is still a comforting memory to look back on. Even with how dissatisfied I am with the current state of Steel Wool and the crude way the story, which I believe to be one of the most tragically beautiful stories ever, has been handled, I still treasure this game very deeply. I can thank my love of horror, my love for costumes and cosplay, even my desire to pursue a career in theatre all back to this game, its characters, and its story.

Thank you, Scott Cawthon, for making a game that changed my life. God bless you and your family.

These characters will live on. In the hearts of children, and adults, they will live on.

This game. What a classic. I'm clearly biased, as this was my childhood, and I vividly remember watching Markiplier's very first Five Nights at Freddy's Let's Play when it came out. My dad watched them along with me, just because he found the reactions funny.

I'm going to try to be as unbiased as possible here, though. This game is pure genius. The premise, which was quite unique at the time, scared the living hell out of many. The ambiance is incredible, mixing childlike wonder with genuine fear. And yes, despite what some might say, this game IS scary. Although not for the jumpscares themselves, but the anticipation. Also the animatronic designs are legit creepy at times. Phenomenal example of a developer playing his weaknesses and small budget as his strengths. Look at where the franchise is now!

10/5. And that's just for the gameplay, ok? Don't even get me started on the story.

I didn’t expect much going in — just an old indie horror game with some loud jumpscares.
But holy hell, this game knows how to mess with your nerves.

No guns. No running. Just doors, lights, cameras... and dread.
You sit in one room all night, completely helpless, praying you don’t hear footsteps or Freddy’s laugh.
And when things go wrong — it’s your fault. That’s what makes it so intense.

Every second is a panic attack waiting to happen.
Foxy ruined my confidence. Freddy ruined my silence. Bonnie and Chica just wouldn’t let me breathe.
The game gives you almost no time to relax — and that’s what makes it so good.

I finished the whole thing in about 5 hours, but it felt like I went to war. Custom Night 20/20/20/20 nearly melted my brain, but beating it felt amazing.

Pros:

Terrifying atmosphere

Minimal mechanics, maximum pressure

No random BS – every mistake is yours

Addictive “just one more try” loop

Cons:
– Not much to do once you beat it
– RNG sometimes kicks you while you're down

If you want a horror game that makes your hands sweat and your brain scream: this is it.

Yes, I recommend this game.
(but don’t be surprised if you start checking your hallway IRL)

Let’s settle something right now, because I’m tired—exhausted, really—of people smugly dismissing Five Nights at Freddy’s like it’s some sort of glitchy carnival sideshow for attention-starved teenagers. “It’s just a bunch of jump scares,” they say, arms folded, brows furrowed, radiating the smug energy of someone who just learned what a “CPU” is and now believes they’re qualified to teach game design at MIT.

Let’s all take a deep, meditative breath through our noses, exhale through our disbelief, and talk like adults for a moment—adults who may or may not be hunted by undead animatronic mascots with the personal boundaries of a chainsaw-wielding tax auditor.

First, let’s address the gameplay—the nerve center of this pizza-soaked fever dream. Yes, you are seated. Yes, you stay seated. Yes, your greatest weapons are a set of security cameras, two doors, a pair of flickering lights, and what I can only describe as a deeply strained relationship with a building’s power grid. The horror is not in running, gunning, or stylish backflips off haunted staircases. The horror is in waiting. The horror is in hearing something shuffling just off-camera. The horror is realizing you closed the door too soon, drained your power too fast, and now Freddy is giggling outside your door like a caffeinated ghost clown.

“But there’s barely any movement!” cries the modern gamer, raised on a steady diet of triple-A open-world explosions and emotionally manipulative dog companions. Yes. That’s. The. Point. FNaF is a horror game that marinates you in your own dread. It doesn’t just scare you; it makes you wait to be scared. It’s less “boo!” and more “you know something’s coming, and it will absolutely ruin your entire week when it does.” FNaF is stress in pixel form. It is pure, distilled tension, like a haunted Excel spreadsheet where the pivot table might scream at you.

Now, let’s talk about the graphics, because nothing says “I missed the point” like someone criticizing FNaF’s visuals as being “too simplistic.” Oh no, how dare this indie game made by one guy in his garage not have ray-traced, 4K ultra-realistic textures of Freddy’s bloodstained bowtie? Look, this isn’t Call of Duty: Animatronic Ops. It’s a claustrophobic surveillance sim built to make you feel powerless. The lo-fi style? It’s intentional. It's there to transport you straight into the fluorescent hellscape of a sketchy family restaurant where the pizza is cold and the lawsuits are warm. If you think it looks cheap, you’re probably also the kind of person who thinks The Blair Witch Project needed more CGI.

And please, please, let’s not pretend that the story—or should I say, the epic, sprawling operatic multiverse of deeply unsettling lore—isn’t a factor here. If you think FNaF is just about not dying before 6 AM, then I regret to inform you that you’ve missed an entire subculture, several novels, a VR game, a movie, and enough fan theories to fill a Congressional hearing. The game dared to have layers. It dared to have a purple guy. It dared to hide entire plot arcs in mini-games that looked like they were made in 1983 on a toaster. This isn’t lazy design—it’s bait for obsessive lunatics (read: fans) who will spend five hours on a video essay analyzing the emotional implications of Balloon Boy’s laugh.

Still not convinced? Think FNaF is just for kids? Think again, and think harder. No child under 13 has any business understanding the psychological nuance of a game that teaches you how fear builds—not from gore or volume, but from silence and stillness. It preys on adult anxieties: responsibility, helplessness, minimum-wage jobs that slowly chip away at your soul until one day you’re staring into the dead eyes of a robot chicken while desperately trying to budget electricity. The fact that children play it doesn’t mean it’s childish. That just means kids are braver than you.

And yes, jump scares are part of it. You know what else has jump scares? Every horror movie that ever made you drop your popcorn and question your bladder control. Jump scares are tools. And in FNaF, they are not the only tool—they’re the payoff. You don’t start with fear. You earn it. With every second survived, every flickering light checked, every hallway where you think you saw something twitch. FNaF doesn’t just jump out and shout “boo”—it lurks, it waits, it gestures politely toward the abyss and lets you fall in willingly.

So the next time someone tells you “FNaF is dumb,” nod politely, smile gently, and understand that you’re speaking to someone who got eaten by Foxy once and never recovered emotionally. It’s okay. Not everyone can handle sitting still in a room while a possessed bunny plots their doom. Not everyone is built for subtlety. Some people need their fear spoon-fed to them with orchestral scores and gallons of fake blood.

Five Nights at Freddy’s is a test—not of reflexes, but of patience, perception, and how long you can survive while teetering on the edge of a nervous breakdown. It’s horror for people who understand that the scariest thing in the world isn’t the monster—it’s knowing the monster is right outside your door, and you only have 2% power left.

And that, my dear skeptics, is not stupid. That is genius, dressed in a silly hat, stuffed in a bear suit, and humming a lullaby just before it devours you.

The last time I played [b]Five Nights at Freddy's[/b], it was just some random indie "horror management" game blowing up the internet and mobile app stores.  Fast-forward a decade or so: FNAF is now a franchise, Target's bookshelves sag under dense spin-off novels, my husband's old classmate made a bunch of lore videos and cameoed in the movie adaptation, and both the OG game and I have visible wrinkles. 

[h3]Story + Gameplay[/h3]
As Mike Schmidt, the newest security guard at Freddy Fazbear's Pizzeria, your only job is to survive five increasingly frantic ~9 minute shifts without getting murdered by wandering animatronics.  Confined to a claustrophobic office, you must ration limited power while also spending it to monitor an unintuitive camera feed, check blind spots, and occasionally close one of two electric doors.  If you run out of power too early or if an animatronic enters your office, the game ends with a jumpscare and Mike's death.

[b]Controls.[/b] SteamDeck verified and okay with a controller, but feels better with a mouse. The camera is still awkward AF to navigate all these years later.

[b]Playtime.[/b]  Once you get the rhythm down, it only takes ~50min to beat the first 5 days, which unlocks the "6th Night" and the first of three stars.  One lore-less and sometimes-harrowing "6th night" later, you'll unlock the second star and "Custom Night," which lets you set the "AI Level" for [i]each[/i] animatronic on an easy to insane scale of 0 to 20.  Beating "Custom Night" on 20/20/20/20 unlocks the third star. Good luck.

[b]Settings + Options.[/b]  Nonexistent.

[h3]What Works For Me[/h3]
✅  Environmental storytelling and details.
✅  Scraps of lore.
✅  Great gameplay loop for streamers and stress junkies.

[h3]What Doesn't Work For Me[/h3]
🟥  Still no achievements! 
🟥  "ESC" closes the game rather than opening a menu.
🟥  What's up with the visual streakiness? 
🟥  Fucking Foxy, man. 
🟥  At this point, there's a million guides and no surprises.
🟥  And it's kinda boring. 

[h3]Final Thoughts + Recommendation[/h3]
This was a tricky review to write because I probably wouldn't recommend [b]FNAF[/b] to modern audiences.  I was a bit addicted ten years ago, but it feels formulaic, contrived, and underwhelming in 2025.  If you've never played the first installment of this viral series, then you're better off watching Nicolas Cage's brilliant [i]Willy's Wonderland[/i] instead*. 

But if we take a step back: [b]FNAF[/b] was one of the first single-player games to truly thrive on Twitch because of how original it was at the time.  There's more lore in ~5 minutes of dialogue than in [i]Minecraft[/i].  Anyone who attended a birthday party at Chuck E. Cheese felt validated by the nightmarish setting and concept.  Today the community is overflowing with guides, but back then everything was just speculation and "does Golden Freddy even exist?"

So… do I recommend this?  Yes, but no.  [list]
[*] If you’ve played before and want to revisit, no; preserve the memory.
[*] If you've never played a FNAF game, skip this one.
[*] If you've played other FNAF games, sure, go for it.
[*] If you're interested in game history or review comps, then YES. 
[/list]

In celebration of the VR addition to [b] Guinness’ “Most Game Sequels Released in a Year” World Record holder [/b] (the Five Nights at Freddy’s franchise), I revisited the game that started it all: [b] Five Nights at Freddy’s 1 (2014).[/b] The franchise evolved over the years, spawning more advanced sequels, many fan-made games, books and other media. But before gamers experience the newest incarnation of FNAF, here’s a quick review of the first game:


[h1]“Night of the Living Mascots:
A Five Nights at Freddy’s Game Review”[/h1]
“Looking for a fright? Come and stay the night, at Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza …” 
 

	Business establishments use mascots to serve as the “face” of the company. The easily-recognizable symbols appear in ads, commercials, and in front of crowds to entice customers. The customers feel safe knowing there’s a minimum-wage employee within the mascot suit. But what if what’s inside the suit is a malfunctioning, poorly-programmed AI robot endoskeleton? That is the world Five Nights at Freddy’s put players in.

	Players will take the role of a night guard in Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza, a seemingly normal pizzeria during the day. Freddy the Bear, the lead singer of an all-robot band, is the pizzeria’s main attraction. Watching over said AI robots or “animatronics” is part of the job description. The problem is those animatronics don’t like humans in the pizzeria after closing hours, delivering a painful death to anyone caught. [spoiler] You’ll be forcibly stuffed into a mascot suit, but it is filled with gears and metalwork. [/spoiler] The only defense mechanism players are provided is a very limited electric supply that powers surveillance cameras, lights and the two doors to the guard’s office. Gameplay is set entirely in the said office, and players just need timing, strategy and observation skills to prevent animatronics from entering. Easy, right? Well … not quite.
 
	Five Nights at Freddy’s 1 seems pretty simple on paper, but that’s where the brilliance of the game comes in. Players are subjected to a first-person psychological thriller, communicated through a genius mix of auditory and visual elements. The only music in the entire game is found in the main menu, and it is very creepy. In the actual gameplay, sounds are used entirely to alert players of an animatronic’s presence; meaning every hustle or footstep can mean life or death. The game developer crafted the fun and cheerful mascots of the pizzeria into eerie night monsters that attack at random. The empty corridors, hallways and rooms viewed through the cameras all add to the scary vibe of the night. Five Nights at Freddy’s captures the thrill of modern games like Fortnite, Rules of Survival, The Forest, and the Resident Evil 2 remake that keeps players on the edge of their seats. So what’s stopping the night guard from quitting? Aside from the salary, there’s a high chance it may be the simple yet beautifully-told story.
 
	Most of the story is exposed via a set of recorded messages left by the previous night guard. Despite his casual tone, the information he gives makes the player’s brain want to uncover the creepy truth behind the pizzeria’s mystery. [spoiler] As the nights progress, some signs seen on camera change to newspaper clippings that reveal more about the story.[/spoiler] All games in the Five Nights at Freddy’s franchise tell an interconnected story, but the plot of Five Nights at Freddy’s 1 is wholesome enough to stand alone. It captivates a player to keep playing in hopes of discovering the complete story that the game offers. The game also rewards players who replay the game with various easter eggs and mini-games.
 
	Critics may say the game pales in comparison to newer releases, but Five Nights at Freddy’s 1 remains a classic for gamers who like horror games. Unlike recent horror games, Five Nights at Freddy’s scares the sh*t out of the player without needing gruesome death illustrations, a feat not many games can do. The game might be repetitive and monotonous, but not everyone can do the one job it requires players to do: [b]survive.[/b]

Really solid indie horror title that still stands up to modern standards, even against this game's own sequels and prequels it stands out. The first installment in the "Five Nights at Freddy's" franchise is an experience that no true gamer should miss out on. As an introduction to the series, it excels by allowing you to experience the horror of the animatronics while not giving you many details behind what is truly driving and motivating these fearsome enemies to attacks. 
While this game stands out for its personality, innovation to the horror genre, and tone of ambiance, it also comes with its fair share of negatives. The by far most egregious negative, and really the only truly notable one in a game priced at 5 dollars, is most definitely the difficulty. 

I LOVE this game, however I can't deny the fact that it is simply too difficult. Only the most hardcore of gamers are going to make it far in this game. This is a game that you can tell was not properly balanced. Both Bonnie and Chica are extremely difficult to handle, and even now I'm still not 100% percent sure on how to deal with them. Foxy seems to be a completely random element with no consistency, and Freddy is literally never active. Seriously, I've never once seen him leave the stage. He is just there to kill you if you run out of power, which seems like a waste of character modeling. Although, the game is hard enough already so adding another factor could easily ruin the game. However, the worst part is: there is no tutorial or introduction. You are told nothing about anything and are expected to just ride right through the game. Unfortunately, this one major negative does exist but it doesn't change how good the game is.

All in all, this game, even with its extreme difficulty, truly shows how much a games artistic design and aesthetic matter. I would definitely recommend to anyone with an interest in horror games. [h1]Most people don't last this long. I mean, you know, they usually move on to other things by now. I'm not implying that they died. [/h1]
[i]Five Nights at Freddy's[/i] is a strange game in that it has at once attracted a cult following and simultaneously that cult has grown into a gargantuan horde. The game is particularly notable for its variety of YouTube reaction scream-a-thons, some of which are better done than others. I was approaching it with a particular amount of cynicism - surely, I thought, this thing, so well-mined, a thing so known, could not provide any scares. But, for about 45 minutes to an hour, it provided tension and even a solid jump scare or two before the magic wore off - which is pretty good for a buck.

I did enjoy watching some of the Let's Plays regarding this game, particularly to see the different strategies and reactions that people had, and what comforted people while playing. For those who've never played or bothered to read about this game (primarily because of the rabid and, as is my understanding, very strange fanbase), you play as a security guard guarding the world's worst pizzeria, as it is inhabited by several roaming animatronics. These animatronics have a few different behaviours, which makes playing the game an exercise in adaptation. The first night, only the rabbit Bonnie is really active, and I quickly determined how to beat him. But when you start to add more of the bloody things to the mix, things start to become genuinely stressful. You have to manage your power so that the doors stay down and you can afford to protect yourself from the giant robots in "cute"(?!?!) costumes wandering the place. 

So it's a very simple idea (though I do wonder why whoever owns this restaurant doesn't renegotiate their contract with the power company) that is pulled off very well. What you can see of the restaurant is claustrophobic, and has shifting elements - things strangely change, text changes, and the animatronics move around a lot, and sometimes even stare into the cameras. 

The game isn't very long, but I did get it for very cheap. I have one night left to beat (though there are extra nights, if you're keen to really challenge yourself and get your full money's worth) and the game does get more difficult as it goes on, as the animatronics get more erratic and things start to get eerier. But it's not for everyone. Despite the setting and animatronics acting up in stranger and stranger ways, the game becomes less scary as you adapt to what's going on. It is very easy to develop a strategy for the game, and mostly stick with it. Freddy (the bear) definitely disrupts things the most, and his first appearance in the camera after he'd moved was easily the most bone-chilling moment I had in the game. 

Overall, a great way to get a quick horror fix, but contains very little of substance beyond what I understand is now a huge backstory - but to get the most of that, investing in the rest of the series is probably required, and most people who'd be interested in that these days have already bought it and ravenously devoured every scrap of information regarding the game. I won't be going as far as them, but the first game is a great little indie horror title.

It's hard to believe that it has been so long since the first game came out. How long it has been has scared in me in a way no Animatronic Bear ever has. It's aged incredibly well and is a masterclass in horror, atmosphere, visuals, and sound design.

I played the demo of this before the full version was released on Steam. Believe me when I say it is one of the most terrifying horror games ever made and it really is as scary as most people make it out to be. The way it plays with your head and toys with you makes you feel so vulnerable and isolated, it isn't like anything else I've felt in any other horror game.

What makes this game so unique is two things: its gameplay, and how you have to survive. Normally in horror games you've got the ability to roam around the map, run, hide and pick up items to help improve your odds of survival. Not in this. You're confined to just one room with a device that lets you take a look at the camera feeds throughout the pizzaria, and in this one room are two doors to the left and to the right, both of which are JUST out of your peripheral vision. You've also got a light for each doorway, since it's completely pitch black through them, so that you can see what is through the doorway (trust me when I say you'll be needing to use those lights very often).

Here you might say "well why can't I just close these two doors for the whole night and not have to bother looking at the cameras or turning the lights on?" It drains the power quite rapidly. If you drain the power early, it's game over... just not instantly. Because of this, you want to conserve as much of your power as you can, which means you won't have the option of keeping either of the doors closed for the whole time, nor the option to keep the lights on. This is where the game becomes pretty terrifying. And then there's Freddy and his pals... 

It'll be easy for those who want action in their games to dismiss this title, since you are only in one room for the whole game. But holy shit do things become tense very early and very quickly. If you are a horror fan, this is an ESSENTIAL title that you NEED to play.

Scott still knows how to evoke a sense of fear and dread between the background noise and the impending danger. Everything is very eerie in general. If you don't figure out the backstory, you'll have it spoiled to you. It's by far the most uncomfortable part of the game. Like Undertale, let the experience be your own and have fun with it. I reminisce about the days when only the first game existed and people had wild theories, just based on a single game. Nowadays I don't have any clue where the plot and theories have went, but Fnaf always felt like a community project, where we as players put the puzzle pieces together.
I never played this game because I didn't have a pc and I didn't want to pay for the mobile port, so the game itself was experienced through let's play videos. Now as an adult I have a computer and money, so I had to play this game for the first time and see if it still holds up.
Looking back at this entry, the first game was scarier than I remebered. You are thrown into a hellish job with minimun wage, where 4 animatronics want to stuff you into a Freddy suit, where wires rip your skin and you die. To prevent this from happening you have a trusty camera system, that lets you monitor the map. Your second method to survive are the doors, that help you when you are in immediate danger. Both of these actions drain power which is limited and runs out fast. If you don't manage the power usage, you will be in the dark and Freddy will scare you. You win by reaching 6 AM. This is basically the gameplay portion, simple and unique. This game was really unique back in the day and it gave birth to the mascot horror genre.
The original animatronics are still my personal favorite ones. They didn't look over the top like in Fnaf 4 and they are genuinely scary, because they look like something you could actually see in a scary pizzeria. Scott had nightmares of Bonnie and I can see why, because he is the most aggresive one. Bonnie is constantly terrorising you by moving fast and jamming your door. In my opinion, Chica looks a little bit goofy but in a good way. She isn't as aggressive as Bonnie and she feels like she is just trolling you by moving near the right door and not trying to attack. Then we have Foxy who sings songs and joggs to your office. If you never look at the cams, he will go active. Lastly we have Freddy, who is a pain to monitor, he moves when you aren't looking at him and when he is at the door, you can't get rid of him.
These enemies make this game really hectic and you are really paranoid all the time. Everyone behaves differently and all in all, you feel like you are trying to overcome a challenge, where the odds are against you.
The athmosphere and ambience is something I never noticed before. This is really good sound design and can't be experienced by watching videos.
Fnaf 1 still holds up in my opinion. There isn't a dull moment and it offers the right amount of challenge even for casual gamers. Everyone who was there, when this game came out will understand how nostalgic it is to sit in this office. If you never tried Fnaf 1, I recommend it. The only gripe I have, is that this game is a jumpscarefest. It might not be for everyone. Especially at the end where you might die a couple of times, which can get old. I might be biased and I just don't get it why do you want to stay, five nights at Freddy's.
bear man kill minimum wage security boy with his goofy ahh friends. 10/10 good.
The classic FNAF 1... great Audio clues, performance on older PCs and for its time THE greatest horror game.

I know I’m a bit late to this, but this game was a huge part of my childhood. I played it a lot when I was about 10. It was actually the first horror game I ever got into. I didn’t have a gaming PC back then, so I just played it on my iPad instead. I finally gave the original PC version a try, and I really liked it, tbh. Even when I know exactly what is coming, it still manages to feel creepy, scary and fun. If you like horror games, I highly recommend it! 11/10

This game uses a simple mechanic (looking at cameras) to create one of the scariest games I have played all year. Even after an hour or two you still will dread looking down from the camera for fear of an Animatronic hiding behind it. Can get very difficult and you are guaranteed to have many close calls as you try to make it through the nights.

At $5 this game is a steal.
It's no Chipper & Sons, but it's a neat little game. I look forward to what Scott has cooking up next in the year 2015.

I believe this game is highly family friendly, all children alike should buy this, the parents AND their kids will love this game, with its quirky robots that talk to your character, 10/10 highly reccomended!
